section.title: oosqlSetAuthorizer
section.para: Registers a routine that is called while SQL is prepared, to allow or deny each action the SQL would do.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call for each action, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its sixth argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error.

The routine is called with six arguments: the action, one of the Authorizer Action Code constants, such as SELECT, READ, or DELETE; two strings that depend on the action, such as the name of the table and of the column; the name of the database; the name of the trigger or view that causes the action; and the user data. The strings that do not apply are empty. The routine must return one of the Authorizer Return Code constants: OK to allow the action, IGNORE to ignore it, for a column read it reads NULL, or DENY to make the preparation fail with AUTH (23), not authorized.
The routine is called when the SQL is prepared, not when it is executed. It must not use the connection.
The functionality of the oosqlSetAuthorizer routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_set_authorizer API.
The setAuthorizer method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also authorizerCallBack.

This example forbids deleting rows:
rc = oosqlSetAuthorizer(db, 'noDelete') say oosqlExec(db, "DELETE FROM foods WHERE id = 1;") rows. = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT name FROM foods WHERE id = 1;", .true) say rows.1['NAME'] rc = oosqlSetAuthorizer(db, '') /* Output: SQLite Error: rc = 23, not authorized Bagels */
::routine noDelete public use arg action, arg1, arg2, dbName, trigger if action == .ooSQLite~DELETE then return .ooSQLite~DENY return .ooSQLite~OK

section.title: oosqlSql
section.para: Returns the SQL text of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
The text of the SQL statement, as it was given to oosqlPrepare. When the text given to oosqlPrepare held more than one statement, only the first one is returned, because only that one was prepared.
The text does not change when values are bound to the parameters: the parameters are still shown as they were written.
The functionality of the oosqlSql routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_sql API.
The sql method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example executes, one by one, all the statements in a string. It uses the _tail argument of oosqlPrepare to get what follows each statement, and displays each statement before executing it:
sql = "CREATE TABLE t(a); INSERT INTO t VALUES(1); INSERT INTO t VALUES(2);" do while sql <> '' rc = oosqlPrepare(db, sql~strip, 'stmt', 'sql') if rc <> .ooSQLite~OK then leave if oosqlIsHandleNull(stmt) then leave -- only blanks or comments were left say oosqlSql(stmt) rc = oosqlStep(stmt) call oosqlFinalize stmt end /* Output: CREATE TABLE t(a); INSERT INTO t VALUES(1); INSERT INTO t VALUES(2); */

section.title: oosqlStatus
section.para: Retrieves runtime status information about the performance of SQLite, and optionally resets its highwater mark.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
op [required]
The status parameter to retrieve, one of the Status Parameter constants, such as STATUS_MEMORY_USED.
result [required]
A Stem object, not the name of a stem, in which the values are returned. Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if it is not a Stem object. On success, these tails of the stem are set: CURRENT, the current value of the parameter, and HIGHWATER, its highest recorded value.
reset [optional]
If true, the highwater mark is reset to the current value after it is retrieved. The default is false.
Returns OK on success, or MISUSE if op is not a valid status parameter. On error, the stem is not changed.

The values are for the whole process, not for a database connection: see oosqlDbStatus for those. Some parameters do not record the highest value, and others record only the highest value; for parameters that do not record the highest value, reset is ignored.
The functionality of the oosqlStatus routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_status API.
The status method of the ooSQLite class does the same, with a Directory object instead of a stem.

This example displays how much memory SQLite is using, and how many allocations it has:
rc = oosqlStatus(.ooSQLite~STATUS_MEMORY_USED, s.) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then say 'Memory used:' s.current 'bytes, highest:' s.highWater 'bytes' rc = oosqlStatus(.ooSQLite~STATUS_MALLOC_COUNT, s.) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then say 'Allocations:' s.current', highest:' s.highWater /* Output might be: Memory used: 63688 bytes, highest: 63712 bytes Allocations: 136, highest: 137 */

section.title: oosqlStep
section.para: Executes a prepared statement, or advances it to its next result row.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.

One of the Result Code constants. The most common ones are ROW, when a new result row is ready, and its values can be retrieved with the oosqlColumn routines; DONE, when the statement has run to completion: there are no more rows, or, for a statement that returns no data, it has been executed; and BUSY, when the database is locked by another connection, and the statement can be stepped again later, see oosqlBusyTimeOut and oosqlBusyHandler.

Any other code is an error, which oosqlErrMsg describes. ooSQLite enables extended result codes for every connection, so the code is often an extended one, such as CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE (2067) for a duplicate value in a UNIQUE column, rather than CONSTRAINT (19).

A statement that returns data, such as a SELECT, is stepped once for each result row, and once more to get DONE. A statement that returns no data, such as an INSERT, is executed by a single step, which returns DONE on success. After DONE or an error, do not step the statement again before resetting it.
The functionality of the oosqlStep routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_step API.
The step method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example displays all the rows of a query, and checks that it ended without error:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name FROM foods ORDER BY name;", 'stmt') do forever rc = oosqlStep(stmt) if rc <> .ooSQLite~ROW then leave say oosqlColumnText(stmt, 1) end if rc <> .ooSQLite~DONE then say 'Error' rc':' oosqlErrMsg(db) call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlStmtBusy
section.para: Tests if a prepared statement has been stepped, but has not run to completion and has not been reset.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle can be null.
Returns true if oosqlStep has been invoked at least once, and the statement has neither returned DONE nor been reset. Otherwise, and for a null handle, returns false.
The functionality of the oosqlStmtBusy routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_stmt_busy API.
The stmtBusy method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example shows the value of oosqlStmtBusy, and of oosqlStmtReadonly, while a query is executed:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name FROM foods;", 'stmt') say oosqlStmtReadonly(stmt) oosqlStmtBusy(stmt) -- 1 0 rc = oosqlStep(stmt) say oosqlStmtBusy(stmt) -- 1 rc = oosqlReset(stmt) say oosqlStmtBusy(stmt) -- 0 call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlStmtReadonly
section.para: Tests if a prepared statement makes no direct changes to the database.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
Returns true if the statement does not write to the database, such as a SELECT, and false if it can, such as an INSERT, an UPDATE, or a DELETE.

A statement can be read only and still change the database indirectly, through a user defined function that executes SQL of its own. Transaction control statements, such as BEGIN and COMMIT, are read only, because they make no changes by themselves.
The functionality of the oosqlStmtReadonly routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_stmt_readonly API.
The stmtReadonly method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlStmtBusy.

section.title: &changed11;oosqlStmtStatus
section.para: Returns the value of one of the performance counters of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
op [required]
The counter to return, one of the Status Parameter (stmt) constants, such as STMTSTATUS_FULLSCAN_STEP or STMTSTATUS_VM_STEP.
reset [optional]
If true, the counter is set to 0 after its value is returned. The default is false.
The value of the counter. For an op that is not one of the constants, 0 is returned, and nothing is reset.
The counters accumulate over all the executions of the statement, also after a reset, until they are reset with the reset argument. They can help find out whether a query would benefit from an index.
The functionality of the oosqlStmtStatus routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_stmt_status API.
The stmtStatus method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example runs a query and displays some of its counters. There is no index on the price column, so the whole table is scanned, and the result has to be sorted:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name FROM foods WHERE price > 1 ORDER BY name;", 'stmt') do while oosqlStep(stmt) == .ooSQLite~ROW end say 'Full scan steps:' oosqlStmtStatus(stmt, .ooSQLite~STMTSTATUS_FULLSCAN_STEP) say 'Sorts: ' oosqlStmtStatus(stmt, .ooSQLite~STMTSTATUS_SORT) say 'VM steps: ' oosqlStmtStatus(stmt, .ooSQLite~STMTSTATUS_VM_STEP, .true) say 'VM steps now: ' oosqlStmtStatus(stmt, .ooSQLite~STMTSTATUS_VM_STEP) call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: Full scan steps: 3 Sorts: 1 VM steps: 47 VM steps now: 0 */

section.title: &changed11;oosqlTableColumnMetadata
section.para: Retrieves metadata about a column of a table of a database connection.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to an open database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
tableName [required]
The name of the table. It must be a table, not a view. The name is case insensitive.
columnName [required]
The name of the column. The name is case insensitive. The names rowid, oid, and _rowid_ are accepted for the rowid of the table.
results [required]
A Stem object, not the name of a stem, in which the metadata are returned. Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if it is not a Stem object. On success, these tails of the stem are set:
DATATYPE
The declared type of the column, or the empty string if the column was declared without a type.
COLLATIONSEQUENCE
The name of the default collation sequence of the column.
NOTNULL
True if the column has a NOT NULL constraint, otherwise false.
PRIMARYKEY
True if the column is part of the primary key, otherwise false.
AUTOINCREMENT
True if the column is AUTOINCREMENT, otherwise false.
dbName [optional]
The name of the database: main, temp, or the name of an attached database. If it is omitted, or is the empty string, all the databases of the connection are searched, in the order SQLite uses for a table name that is not qualified.

Returns OK on success, or ERROR if the table or the column does not exist, or the table is a view; oosqlErrMsg describes the error, for example no such table column: foods.weight. On error, the stem is not changed.

When columnName names the rowid, and the table has a column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, the metadata of that column is returned. When it has none, the metadata is: data type INTEGER, collation sequence BINARY, not null false, primary key true, and auto increment false.

The functionality of the oosqlTableColumnMetadata routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_table_column_metadata API. The order of the arguments is not the same: the optional database name is the last one.
The tableColumnMetadata method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same, with a Directory object instead of a stem.

This example displays the metadata of some columns of the foods table, and then asks for a column that does not exist:
do col over .array~of('id', 'name', 'price', 'rowid') rc = oosqlTableColumnMetadata(db, 'foods', col, m.) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then say col~left(6) m.dataType~left(8) m.collationSequence - m.notNull m.primaryKey m.autoIncrement end rc = oosqlTableColumnMetadata(db, 'foods', 'weight', m.) say rc oosqlErrMsg(db) /* Output: id INTEGER BINARY 0 1 0 name TEXT BINARY 0 0 0 price REAL BINARY 0 0 0 rowid INTEGER BINARY 0 1 0 1 no such table column: foods.weight */

section.title: oosqlTotalChanges
section.para: Returns the number of rows changed, inserted, or deleted since a database connection was opened.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
The number of rows.

The count includes the changes made by triggers and by foreign key actions, but not those made to carry out REPLACE constraints, rollbacks, or DROP TABLE. oosqlChanges counts the changes of the last statement only.
The functionality of the oosqlTotalChanges routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_total_changes API.
The totalChanges method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.
See the example of oosqlChanges.

section.title: oosqlTrace
section.para: Registers a routine that is called with the text of each SQL statement when it starts executing.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call for each statement, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its second argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns the userData of the routine that was registered before, or .nil if there was none, or it had no user data.

The routine is called with two arguments: the SQL text, and the user data. When a trigger starts, it is also called, with a comment that names the trigger as the SQL text. It must return a whole number, which is ignored.
A connection has only one of trace and profile routine: registering one removes the other.
The functionality of the oosqlTrace routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_trace API.
The trace method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also traceCallBack.

This example displays each statement executed by a call to oosqlExec, with a prefix given as the user data:
rc = oosqlTrace(db, 'showSql', 'SQL>') rc = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT count(*) FROM foods; UPDATE foods SET price = 3 WHERE id = 1;") rc = oosqlTrace(db, '') /* Output: SQL> SELECT count(*) FROM foods; SQL> UPDATE foods SET price = 3 WHERE id = 1; */
::routine showSql public use arg sql, prefix say prefix sql return 0

section.title: oosqlUpdateHook
section.para: Registers a routine that is called whenever a row is inserted, updated, or deleted.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call for each row changed, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its fifth argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns the userData of the routine that was registered before, or .nil if there was none, or it had no user data.

The routine is called with five arguments: the operation, which is one of the Authorizer Action Code constants INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE; the name of the database, such as main; the name of the table; the rowid of the row, after the change for an update; and the user data. It must return a whole number, which is ignored.

The routine is not called for changes to tables without a rowid, to internal tables, or for the rows deleted by a DELETE without a WHERE clause, which SQLite carries out by truncating the table. It must not use the connection: it must not prepare or execute SQL on it.
The functionality of the oosqlUpdateHook routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_update_hook API.
The updateHook method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also updateHookCallBack.

This example displays the rows changed by an UPDATE and a DELETE:
rc = oosqlUpdateHook(db, 'showChange') rc = oosqlExec(db, "UPDATE foods SET price = 2 WHERE type_id = 1; DELETE FROM foods WHERE id = 3;") rc = oosqlUpdateHook(db, '') /* Output: UPDATE main.foods rowid 1 UPDATE main.foods rowid 2 DELETE main.foods rowid 3 */
::routine showChange public use arg op, dbName, tableName, rowid select when op == .ooSQLite~INSERT then what = 'INSERT' when op == .ooSQLite~UPDATE then what = 'UPDATE' otherwise what = 'DELETE' end say what dbName'.'tableName 'rowid' rowid return 0
